title: Cost Visibility Dashboard
subtitle: Build the system that catches a cloud bill going wrong — while there's still time to stop it.
intro: The problem. A business estimates $5,000/month. The first bill is $8,000. Nobody notices. Three months later it's $30,000 and the money is gone. Nothing failed and nobody was hacked — the bill just grew where nobody was looking. You're building the smoke detector for that.

phases.title: Baseline
phases.blurb: Evidence of the 'before'. These can never be retaken once resources exist.

steps.title: How to read these tasks
steps.what: Every Terraform task in this lab is the same shape. Learn it once here and the other eleven are the same job with different words.
steps.why: The point of this page is that you stop needing step-by-step direction. Once the pattern is in your head, a task like "create a storage account with versioning" is enough.

head: Part
What it means
rows: The keyword. You are declaring a thing that should exist.
The type. Comes from the provider. Never invented — always looked up.
The local name. Yours to pick. Only used to reference it elsewhere in your own code.
The arguments. Which ones exist, and which are required, is in the docs for that type.

steps.callout: Where everything lives. All Terraform for this lab goes in projects/01-cost-visibility/terraform/. One file per concern: main.tf (foundation, identity, storage), monitoring.tf (alerts), budget.tf, export.tf, outputs.tf. Terraform reads every .tf file in the folder and treats them as one config, so the split is purely for humans. Write each task where its TODO marker already sits.

hints.label: How do I find the arguments?
hints.text: Go to the azurerm provider docs. Use the search box on the left. Type the resource type, for example resource_group. Open it. Two sections matter: Example Usage, which is copyable shape, and Argument Reference, which tells you what is Required versus Optional. Required arguments are the only ones you strictly need; the rest are choices you are making on purpose.

hints.label: How do I point one resource at another?
hints.text: Use type.local_name.attribute. So the resource group you declare as resource "azurerm_resource_group" "main" is referenced elsewhere as azurerm_resource_group.main.name or .location or .id. This matters for more than typing. Referencing is how Terraform learns the order to build things in. If you hardcode the string "rg-costvis" instead, Terraform has no idea the two are related and may try to build them in the wrong order. Which attributes exist is listed under Attributes Reference on each docs page.

hints.label: What is the loop?
hints.text: Write a block, then run ./scripts/check.sh. It shows remaining TODOs, runs terraform fmt, and runs terraform validate. Nothing touches Azure and nothing costs money, so run it as often as you like. Validate catches wrong argument names, missing required arguments, and type errors. It does not catch a value that is legal but wrong, which is what the requirement checks at the end are for. Expect validation to fail until the last task is done, because workbook.tf references resources you have not written yet. That is normal.

hints.label: What if I get stuck?
hints.text:
In order: read the error, since Terraform names the file, line, and usually the exact argument. Then check the docs page for that resource. Then open the Level 1 hint on the task. Then use the tutor button on the step, which can read your actual file and tell you what is wrong.

Asking the tutor is not cheating. Opening Level 3 and copying the code without understanding it is the only thing that defeats the purpose.

phases.title: Foundation
phases.blurb: Open terraform/main.tf and work top to bottom. Terraform in one sentence: you describe what you want, and it makes Azure match.

steps.title: Resource group
steps.what: A folder. Everything in this lab goes inside it, and deleting the folder deletes everything in it.
steps.real: This is exactly why cloud bills spiral. People create things in random places, forget them, and pay for years. One folder per project means one command cleans it all up.
steps.why: Tags are how you answer 'what did this project cost?'. Untagged resources are the reason companies can't attribute their own spending.

hints.label: Point me in the right direction
hints.text: Search azurerm_resource_group at the registry and open Example Usage. It needs three arguments and nothing more.

hints.label: Show me the shape (values blank)
hints.text: name, location, tags. Use string interpolation for the name so the prefix stays configurable.

hints.label: Show me the code

annotated.note: Start of the block. `azurerm_resource_group` is the kind of thing being made. `"main"` is my own nickname for it, used when other code needs to point at this one. Azure never sees the nickname.
The name Azure actually shows. `${...}` drops a variable into the string. `var.name_prefix` is `costvis`, so this comes out as `rg-costvis`.
Which Azure region it lives in. Comes from a variable so I change it in one place instead of nine.
Labels stuck on the resource. These are what let me answer "what did this project cost" later. Untagged resources are invisible in a cost breakdown.

steps.title: Log Analytics workspace
steps.what: Where logs go so you can search them later. Without it, logs are written and thrown away.
steps.real: This is what you'd search after an incident to answer 'who accessed that, and when?'. Here it records who read your cost data.
props: location and resource_group_name — reference the group from 1.1 rather than retyping it
steps.why: Writing azurerm_resource_group.main.name instead of the literal string tells Terraform this depends on that, so it builds them in the right order automatically.
steps.callout: Answer this in DECISIONS.md: retention defaults to 30 days, not the 730-day maximum. Why deliberately keep less?

hints.label: Point me in the right direction
hints.text: Search azurerm_log_analytics_workspace. The SKU you want is the pay-as-you-go one, and retention is measured in days.

hints.label: Show me the shape (values blank)
hints.text: name, location, resource_group_name, sku, retention_in_days, tags.
hints.code:
resource "azurerm_log_analytics_workspace" "main" {
  name                = 
  location            = 
  resource_group_name = 

  sku               = 
  retention_in_days = 

  tags = 
}

hints.label: Show me the code
hints.code:
resource "azurerm_log_analytics_workspace" "main" {
  name                = "law-${var.name_prefix}"
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.main.location
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.main.name

annotated.note: Creates the place logs get sent. Without something like this, logs are generated and thrown away.
Becomes `law-costvis`. Same variable trick as before.
Reuses the resource group's region instead of me typing the region again. Pointing at another resource also tells Terraform to build that one first.
Puts this workspace inside the folder from 1.1.
The pricing plan. `PerGB2018` means pay per gigabyte of logs taken in. The first 5 GB each month is free, and this lab uses a tiny fraction of that.
How many days logs are kept before Azure deletes them. Longer retention costs more, so 30 days is a deliberate choice, not a default.
Same labels as everything else in the project.

phases.title: Identity and access
phases.blurb: The security core of the lab.

steps.title: Managed identity
steps.what: A login for software instead of a person. No password exists, so no password can leak.
steps.real: The classic breach: a developer hardcodes a password, pushes it to GitHub, and a bot finds it within minutes. A managed identity removes the password entirely — Azure handles it invisibly.

hints.label: Point me in the right direction
hints.text: Search azurerm_user_assigned_identity. It takes the same four basics as the resource group plus a location.

hints.label: Show me the shape (values blank)
hints.text: name, location, resource_group_name, tags.

hints.label: Show me the code

annotated.note: Creates a login for software rather than a person. Nothing about it has a password, which means there is no password to accidentally commit to GitHub.
Becomes `id-costvis-reader`. The name says what it is allowed to do, which matters when you have forty of these.
Region. Same one as everything else.
Lives in the project folder.
Project labels.

steps.title: Role assignment — least privilege
steps.what: The identity above can currently do nothing at all. This grants it exactly one permission: read cost data.
steps.real: Ransomware spreads because service accounts have far more access than they need. One over-permissioned backup account can end a company. Least privilege asks: if this is stolen, what's the worst that happens? Here the answer is 'someone learns what your bill was.'
props: scope — data.azurerm_subscription.current.id. Billing lives at subscription level, not inside your resource group
steps.why: A managed identity has two IDs. principal_id is who it is, used for permissions. client_id is how apps address it. Using the wrong one produces an error that doesn't explain itself.

hints.label: Point me in the right direction
hints.text: Search azurerm_role_assignment. Three arguments: where the permission applies, which permission, and who gets it. Think about which of the identity's two IDs represents who it is.

hints.label: Show me the shape (values blank)
hints.text: scope, role_definition_name, principal_id. The scope is the subscription data source's .id.

hints.label: Show me the code

annotated.note: This is the line that actually grants permission. Until this exists, the identity from 1.3 can do literally nothing.
Where the permission applies. This is the whole subscription, because billing data lives at subscription level. A resource-group scope would not be able to read a bill at all.
Which permission. `Cost Management Reader` is a built-in Azure role that can read cost data and nothing else. Not Contributor, not Owner, not even Reader.

Who gets it. `principal_id` is the identity's object ID, meaning *who it is*. The identity also has a `client_id`, which is how apps address it. Using `client_id` here fails with an error that does not mention `client_id` anywhere.

phases.title: Storage
phases.blurb: 'Misconfigured storage bucket' is one of the most common breach headlines there is. This phase is about not being that.

steps.title: Storage account — the security baseline
steps.what: Cloud file storage. Your daily bill copies land here.
steps.real: Millions of records get exposed this way every year, always the same root cause: someone left a container public. Every setting below is a control that has prevented a real breach somewhere.
props: name — "st${var.name_prefix}${random_string.suffix.result}". No hyphens allowed, and it must be globally unique across all of Azure
Public access disabled — this is the headline one
A blob_properties block with versioning on and 7-day soft delete for both blobs and containers
steps.why: Versioning plus soft delete is ransomware defense. Ransomware encrypts files by overwriting them. With versioning on, the originals are still there.

hints.label: Point me in the right direction
hints.text: Search azurerm_storage_account. The security arguments are near the top of the docs page; data protection lives inside a nested blob_properties block. One argument name changed in provider v4 — if you use the v3 name you'll get a clear error, so read it.

hints.label: Show me the shape (values blank)
hints.text: https_traffic_only_enabled, min_tls_version, allow_nested_items_to_be_public. Inside blob_properties: versioning_enabled, delete_retention_policy, container_delete_retention_policy.

hints.label: Show me the code

annotated.note: Creates cloud file storage. The daily copies of the bill land here.
Storage account names have to be unique across all of Azure, and allow only lowercase letters and numbers. That is why a random 6-character suffix gets glued on the end.
Standard is the cheap, disk-backed option. Premium is SSD and costs far more for no benefit here.
LRS keeps three copies inside one datacenter. The alternatives copy across regions and cost more to protect data that regenerates daily anyway.
The current generation of storage account. There is no reason to pick an older one.
Refuses plain HTTP. Anything connecting has to use encryption in transit.
Refuses old, breakable encryption. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 have known attacks against them.
This is the big one. It makes it impossible for anyone to flip a container to public. "Misconfigured storage bucket" breaches are this setting being wrong.
Opens a sub-block. Everything inside applies to blobs rather than to the account itself.
Keeps the old copy whenever a file is overwritten. This is ransomware defence: ransomware encrypts by overwriting, and versioning means the originals are still sitting there.
Opens the soft-delete settings for individual files.
A deleted file is recoverable for 7 days instead of being gone instantly.
The same protection, but for someone deleting a whole container rather than one file.
Project labels.

steps.what: Turns on logging for the storage account and sends it to the workspace from 1.2.

Just a label for this logging rule.

Where the logs are sent.

steps.title: Action group
steps.what: The delivery list. Alerts don't send themselves — they hand off to an action group, which emails, texts, or calls.
steps.real: When you need to add your manager to every alert, you change one action group instead of editing every rule and forgetting two.
props: name, resource_group_name, and short_name — "costalert" (max 12 chars; Azure uses it as an SMS prefix)
One email receiver per address in var.alert_emails, each with the common alert schema enabled
steps.why: var.alert_emails is a list. A single hardcoded block only handles one address — you need Terraform's dynamic blocks, which generate one block per list item.

hints.label: Point me in the right direction
hints.text: Search azurerm_monitor_action_group, then look up dynamic blocks. Inside a dynamic block named email_receiver, the iterator is also called email_receiver, with .key and .value.

hints.label: Show me the shape (values blank)
hints.text: name, resource_group_name, short_name, tags, plus a dynamic "email_receiver" with for_each = var.alert_emails and a content block setting name, email_address, use_common_alert_schema.

hints.label: Show me the code

annotated.note: The delivery mechanism. Alerts do not send themselves; they hand off to an action group, which emails, texts, or calls a webhook.
Becomes `ag-costvis`.
Lives in the project folder.
Maximum 12 characters. Azure uses it as the prefix on SMS messages, which is why it is capped so short.
Generates one `email_receiver` block per item in a list. Writing a single hardcoded block would only ever handle one address.
The list being looped over. One receiver gets generated for each address in it.
What each generated block contains. This runs once per list item.
Each receiver needs a unique name, so the list index gets appended: `email-0`, `email-1`, and so on. `email_receiver.key` is that index.
The actual address. `.value` is the current item from the list.
Sends alerts in Azure's standard payload format, so a webhook or ticket system can parse them without custom code per alert type.

steps.title: Cost anomaly alert
steps.what: Azure learns your normal daily spend and tells you when today doesn't match.
steps.real: A monthly budget is slow. If something starts costing $200/day on the 3rd, the budget stays silent until the running total crosses a threshold — maybe two weeks and $2,800 later. The anomaly alert catches the shape changing the next day.

hints.label: Point me in the right direction
hints.text: Search "cost anomaly" at the registry. This one emails directly rather than going through an action group.

resource "azurerm_cost_anomaly_alert" "main" {
  name            = "anomaly-${var.name_prefix}"
  display_name    = "Daily cost anomaly"
  subscription_id = data.azurerm_subscription.current.id
  email_subject   = "Azure cost anomaly detected"

resource "azurerm_consumption_budget_subscription" "main" {
  name            = "budget-${var.name_prefix}"
  subscription_id = data.azurerm_subscription.current.id

  amount     = var.monthly_budget
  time_grain = "Monthly"

  time_period {
    start_date = var.budget_start_date
    end_date   = var.budget_end_date
  }

  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold      = 50.0
    operator       = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    threshold_type = "Actual"
    contact_emails = var.alert_emails
    contact_groups = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.cost.id]
  }

  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold      = 80.0
    operator       = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    threshold_type = "Actual"
    contact_emails = var.alert_emails
    contact_groups = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.cost.id]
  }

  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold      = 100.0
    operator       = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    threshold_type = "Actual"
    contact_emails = var.alert_emails
    contact_groups = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.cost.id]
  }

  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold      = 100.0
    operator       = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    threshold_type = "Forecasted"
    contact_emails = var.alert_emails
    contact_groups = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.cost.id]
  }
}

When the budget is active. Start date has to be UTC midnight on the first of a month.
Fires at 50% of the budget. Informational — just telling me the month is moving.
`GreaterThanOrEqualTo` means fire at or above the threshold, not exactly on it.
Based on money already spent. Backward-looking: by the time this fires, the money is gone.
Addresses emailed directly by the budget.
Also route through the action group from 2.1, so adding SMS later is one change instead of four.
Fires at 80%. This is the "go look at what is running" alert.

steps.title: Daily cost export
steps.what: Azure writes a CSV of your real usage into storage every day.
steps.real: The portal is fine for 'what am I spending now'. It's useless for 'what did this look like in March' once the view resets. The export is your own permanent copy.
props: name, subscription_id, daily recurrence, and the two period dates
An export_data_storage_location block pointing at the container from 1.6, with root_folder_path = "daily"
steps.why: Terraform normally works out order by watching which resources reference each other. This export never mentions the role assignment, so Terraform doesn't know it must wait for permissions — and would happily create an export that silently fails its first run. You have to say it out loud.

hints.label: Point me in the right direction
hints.text: Search azurerm_subscription_cost_management_export. Two nested blocks: where it writes, and what it writes. ActualCost is what was billed; AmortizedCost spreads reservation purchases over time.

hints.label: Show me the shape (values blank)

hints.label: Show me the code

annotated.note: Tells Azure to write a CSV of real usage into storage on a schedule. Cost Analysis in the portal is fine for today; this is how you still have March's numbers in September.
Name of the scheduled export.
Which subscription's costs to export.
Daily. Every day it writes a fresh file.
When the schedule starts running.
When it stops. Has to be in the future or the export never runs.
Opens the block describing where the file goes.
The container from 1.6.
A subfolder inside that container, so the files are not loose at the root.
Opens the block describing what goes in the file.

What was actually billed. The alternative, `AmortizedCost`, spreads big upfront purchases across the months they cover. With no reservations in play they are identical, but ActualCost matches the invoice.

Terraform normally works out order by noticing which resources reference each other, but this export never mentions the role assignment, so it has no idea it has to wait. Without this line it can create an export that silently fails its first run.

phases.title: Verify every control
phases.blurb: Terraform saying 'created' is not proof a control is on. This is the difference between 'I configured it' and 'I verified it'.

steps.title: Portal verification sweep
steps.what: Five screenshots, one per control, each showing the setting actually enabled.

shots.desc: Resource groups → rg-costvis. Show all resources and the tags.
shots.caption: All resources deployed with project tags

shots.desc: Cost Management → Budgets → budget-costvis. Must show all four conditions including Forecasted.
shots.caption: Budget with three actual thresholds and a forecast alert

shots.desc: Storage account → Configuration. Secure transfer Enabled, minimum TLS 1.2.
shots.caption: Storage enforcing HTTPS-only and TLS 1.2

shots.desc: Storage account → Data protection. Versioning on, soft delete 7 days.
shots.caption: Blob versioning and 7-day soft delete enabled

shots.desc: Managed identity → Azure role assignments. Exactly one role.
shots.caption: Identity holds only Cost Management Reader

phases.title: Prove the control works
phases.blurb: The most important phase, and the one almost nobody does.

steps.title: Test that least privilege denies
steps.what: Sign in as the managed identity and try something outside its role. It must fail. Then read cost data, which must succeed.
steps.real: This is what a security audit actually asks for. Not 'is MFA enabled' but 'show me a login being blocked'. Evidence beats configuration.
steps.callout: Tell me when you reach this step and I'll give you the exact commands. They depend on values from your apply outputs.

shots.desc: Terminal showing AuthorizationFailed when the identity attempts a write.
shots.caption: Identity denied when attempting an action outside its role

shots.desc: Terminal showing the same identity successfully reading cost data.
shots.caption: Same identity permitted to read cost data

phases.title: Prove the alert reaches a human
phases.blurb: Budgets evaluate every 12–24 hours, so waiting for a real trigger isn't practical. Test the delivery path directly.

steps.title: Test the action group
steps.what: Portal → Action group ag-costvis → Test action group → Budget alert → Test.
steps.why: The inbox screenshot closes the loop: code → cloud → a human being told. That's the entire point of the system.

shots.desc: The test result showing success.
shots.caption: Action group test succeeded

shots.desc: Your actual inbox with the alert email in it.
shots.caption: Alert email received — full path from Terraform to inbox

phases.title: The dashboard
phases.blurb: Terraform built the workbook shell. The cost charts get added in the portal, because hand-writing the query JSON produces dashboards that silently show nothing.

steps.title: Add the cost tiles
steps.what: Workbook → Edit → Add → Add query → Data source: Azure Resource Manager.

shots.desc: The ARM query configuration in edit mode.
shots.caption: Workbook ARM data source querying Cost Management

shots.desc: The chart actually rendering data.
shots.caption: Cost dashboard rendering live data

shots.desc: Advanced Editor showing the JSON.
shots.caption: Workbook JSON for export back into Terraform

steps.callout: Then paste the JSON to me and I'll fold it into workbook.tf, so the finished dashboard is reproducible from code instead of hand-built.

phases.title: Next day — real data
phases.blurb: Cost data lags 8–24 hours. Come back tomorrow.

shots.desc: Storage → Containers → cost-exports → daily → the CSV Azure wrote.
shots.caption: Daily cost export CSV written to blob storage

shots.desc: Cost analysis now showing BUDGET: $25 and a forecast — the direct counterpart to your baseline shot.
shots.caption: Cost analysis with budget and forecast active

phases.title: Tear it down
phases.blurb: Most portfolios skip this. Doing it demonstrates the exact discipline the project is about.
